clinicalPearls: A relatively mild, non-progressive diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma most common in East Asian populations
Caused by biallelic variants in SERPINB7, a serine protease inhibitor expressed in the stratum corneum
A characteristic feature is transient whitening and spongy swelling of the affected skin on water immersion, resembling an exaggerated aquagenic wrinkling
The keratoderma is transgredient, extending onto the dorsa of the hands and feet, the Achilles region and the wrists, often with erythematous margins
Hyperhidrosis and malodour with secondary dermatophyte and pitted-keratolysis-type infection are common
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by the water-immersion sign and SERPINB7 molecular testing, and it is distinguished from the more severe Mal de Meleda
Management is supportive with keratolytics, emollients, antiperspirants and treatment of secondary infection
reference.pathophysiology: Nagashima-type palmoplantar keratoderma is caused by loss of function of SERPINB7, a serine protease inhibitor that helps regulate proteolytic activity within the stratum corneum. Its deficiency is thought to impair the water-barrier properties of the cornified layer, so that acral skin absorbs water abnormally and swells and whitens on immersion, and terminal keratinocyte processing is disturbed to give a diffuse transgredient keratoderma. The compromised barrier and associated hyperhidrosis favour secondary microbial colonisation and malodour.
additionalInvestigations: Water-immersion test to demonstrate whitening and swelling
Bacterial swabs where malodour or pitting suggests secondary infection
redFlags: Marked functional impairment or painful fissuring of the soles
Features atypical for the mild course suggesting an alternative, more severe keratoderma
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and non-progressive; with regular keratolytic and emollient care and attention to secondary infection, most patients maintain good function and quality of life.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the more severe and potentially mutilating Mal de Meleda
Overlooking the diagnostic water-immersion whitening sign
Neglecting the treatable dermatophyte and pitted-keratolysis-type infections driving malodour
Assuming progression and prescribing aggressive systemic therapy unnecessarily
